scenarios.name: R1: at setup each seat holds 8 cards and the deck is empty
R2: at setup pile_size is 0 and all catches and caught are 0
R3: round 4 has seat 1 active with rank 4 (true play of 4,4 trusted)
R3: round 6 has seat 3 active with rank 6
R4: active seat with 0 cards is skipped, no k asked, no poll, nothing moves
R5: choosing k=4 with 2 cards plays only 2
R6: required-rank cards are played first, so 5,5 from {1,6,5,5} is true and the lone challenger takes the pile
R7: playing 1,2 when rank 1 is required is a bluff, so the challenged player picks up the pile
R7: playing 1,1 when rank 1 is required is true, so the challenger takes the pile
R8: playing k=3 lowers hand_size by 3 and raises pile_size by 3
R9: the active seat makes a claim of k cards (only the play is checked; the text is not observable)
R10: both non-active seats are polled, including a seat holding 0 cards; the active seat is not polled
R11: a single challenge resolves the play (the reveal itself is not observable)
R12: a bluff challenged by both makes the bluffer take the pile; caught +1 and each challenger's catches +1
R13: a true play challenged by one player gives that challenger the whole pile, with no counters changed
R14: a true play challenged by both on a pile of 7 gives each challenger 3 cards and removes 1
R15: when both players Trust, even a bluff stays in the pile and no hands change
R16: the trusting player gains no cards when the other player challenges a true play
R17: after a round the public counters reflect the round's outcome
R18: the game ends after round 24 (seat 3 empties its hand and wins)
R19: with equal hand_size and equal catches, fewer caught wins
R19: seats level on cards, catches and caught share the win
R19: fewest cards wins outright over more catches

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed the table at 3. The rank schedule (each seat facing two fixed ranks, 8 turns each) and the split rule for two challengers depend on exactly 3 seats, so neither the minimum nor the maximum can move.

spec_choices.what: No all-players talk poll before the Trust/Challenge poll
spec_choices.why: The source gives only the active player one public statement. Adding free talk would add a mechanic; the bluffing lives in the claim and the statement.

spec_choices.what: The statement is a separate ask after k
spec_choices.why: Each question takes one answer type, so the number and the text are asked in two steps by the same seat.
Catches are at most 24 (times 100 is under 10000) and caught is at most 8 (under 100), so the weights reproduce the strict tie-break order: fewest cards, then most catches, then fewest caught.

A thoughtful player tracks how many of each rank have been revealed, picked up or must still be out, judges whether a claim of k is plausible, and weighs taking the pile against letting a rival shed cards. They also choose when an honest play invites a costly challenge, and use the statement to mislead.

simplifications.what: The k cards are chosen by a fixed engine rule rather than by the player
simplifications.why: The source already specifies this; it is carried out as remove/append operations on hand, played and pile.

simplifications.what: Shuffling and splitting the pile are random draws from the pile list
simplifications.why: The engine shuffles by drawing at random, which gives the same result.

simplifications.what: The draw among tied players is a shared win
simplifications.why: The engine has no separate draw; players level at the top share the win.

variation.original_summary: Hogwash is a bluffing shedding game. Players take turns discarding 1 to 4 cards face down, claiming they are the required rank, which rises by one each turn. Any opponent may call 'Hogwash!': a caught bluffer takes the whole pile, a wrong challenger takes it instead, and the first player to empty their hand wins.

review.evidence: In the reviewed 3-seat version (ranks 1-4, six copies, 8 cards each), every seat faces all four ranks within its first four turns. 'Play your true count, always Trust' therefore empties about 97% of hands with no bluffing at all. About 80% of games end in all-zero draws. Every end check falls right after seat 3's turn, which gives seat 3 an edge. The first challenger on a true play takes different cards from the second.

Under sensible play the result is a draw (about 80%) or a round-9 win decided by who was dealt no copies of their fourth rank. Better reading of claims is rarely needed, so it rarely shows up in results.
A near-optimal policy (play honestly, trust plausible claims) is trivially easy, so a strong player has little room to improve. The card-counting inference exists but is almost never needed.
Hidden hands and a face-down pile allow real inference (copies left = total minus your own minus revealed). The rank rotation makes bluffing unnecessary, so that inference seldom decides anything.
Hand sizes, the truth of each play and the winner all follow by counting cards.
The game is turn-based, text-only and has no board. It uses a private number choice, a simultaneous poll and stack operations, and fits in about 11 steps per round over 24 rounds.

problems: P1: Rank rotation lets every seat meet every rank in four turns, so honest play empties hands and bluffing and challenge-reading become unnecessary.
P2: About 80% of games are draws, because several players reach 0 and ties are not broken.
P3: Seat edge: early-end checks only after rounds that are multiples of 3 always fall right after seat 3's turn.
P4: The order of challengers matters on a true play (first takes the top k cards, second takes the next k).

P5: Penalties are too soft and too mechanical. A wrong challenge costs only k cards, and an unchallenged bluff makes trusters take a card. This blunts the original's high-stakes challenge and punishes a correct Trust.
P6: Under good play the winner is set by the deal (who lacked a rank), not by reasoning.

changes.what: Use ranks 1-6 with 4 copies each (24 cards, 8 per player). The required rank in round r is ((r-1) mod 6)+1, so seat 1 always faces ranks 1 and 4, seat 2 faces 2 and 5, and seat 3 faces 3 and 6.
changes.why: Each player holds on average only about 2.7 cards of their two ranks. Roughly two-thirds of every hand can only leave through bluffs, which opponents must read by card counting (only 4 copies of each rank exist).

changes.what: Drop the early-end checks. The game always lasts exactly 24 rounds, so each seat is active 8 times and answers 16 claims.
changes.why: This removes the timing that favoured seat 3 and gives every seat the same number of turns and responses.

changes.what: Restore the original stakes. A caught bluffer takes the whole pile; a wrong lone challenger takes the whole pile. If two players wrongly challenge, the pile is shuffled and split evenly between them, with any odd card removed from the game.
changes.why: Challenging becomes a real gamble whose cost grows with the pile. Seat order no longer decides who takes which cards.

changes.what: Remove the 'unchallenged bluff makes trusters take a card' rule. Trusting never adds cards; unchallenged bluff cards simply stay hidden in the pile.
changes.why: Trust and Challenge become a genuine read of the claimant, as in the original, and false information accumulates in the pile.

changes.what: Add a tiebreak for fewest cards: first, most correct challenges (bluffs caught); then, fewest times caught bluffing; draw only if still tied.
changes.why: Players who reach 0 are separated by their reading skill, and a player at 0 still has a reason to keep making risky challenges.

keeps: Face-down discards with a public claim of quantity and rank
A required rank that advances each turn and wraps around
Anyone may call a challenge; the loser of the challenge takes the whole pile
Free bluffing talk attached to the claim

recommendation.reason: The core bluff-and-call loop is a strong inference game. The problems were the rank rotation, end timing and soft penalties, and all of these can be fixed within the limits.

variation.name: Hogwash: Six Ranks
variation.summary: This is a three-player bluffing shedding game. Each seat only ever faces two ranks, so most cards must be bluffed away. Opponents count cards to decide whether to call, and a wrong call costs the caller the whole pile.
variation.rules:
SETUP. The deck has 24 cards: ranks 1 to 6, four copies of each. Shuffle and deal 8 cards to each of seats 1, 2 and 3. Hands are private. Everyone always knows every hand size and the pile size. The central pile starts empty; its cards are face down. Each player has two public counters starting at 0: CATCHES (correct challenges) and CAUGHT (times caught bluffing).

ROUNDS. The game lasts exactly 24 rounds. In round r the active player is seat ((r-1) mod 3)+1 and the required rank is ((r-1) mod 6)+1. As a result, seat 1 always faces ranks 1 and 4, seat 2 faces ranks 2 and 5, and seat 3 faces ranks 3 and 6. Each seat is active 8 times.

EACH ROUND:
1. Announce the round, the active player and the required rank.
2. If the active player holds 0 cards, they skip; go to step 8. Otherwise the active player privately chooses k from 1 to 4. If k exceeds their hand size, k becomes their hand size. They may add one short public statement, which may be untrue.
3. The engine moves k cards from the active player's hand onto the top of the pile. It takes cards of the required rank first, up to k. If more are needed, it takes cards of the next rank up, then the next, counting 6 as followed by 1. The play is TRUE if all k cards are the required rank; otherwise it is a BLUFF. This is recorded privately.
4. Announce: 'Seat X claims k cards of rank R', plus the statement.
5. Simultaneous poll: each of the two other players secretly chooses Trust or Challenge. The choices are revealed together.
6. If anyone challenged, reveal the k played cards to all.
   (a) If the play was a BLUFF: the active player takes the entire pile into their hand, and the pile becomes empty. The active player's CAUGHT increases by 1. Each challenger's CATCHES increases by 1.
   (b) If the play was TRUE and there was one challenger: that challenger takes the entire pile into their hand.
   (c) If the play was TRUE and there were two challengers: shuffle the pile. Each challenger takes half of it, rounded down. If one card remains, it is removed from the game face down. The pile becomes empty.
7. If both players chose Trust, nothing happens. The cards stay face down in the pile, true or not.
8. Announce every player's hand size, the pile size and all CATCHES and CAUGHT counters.
9. If round 24 has been played, the game ends.

A player holding 0 cards still answers every poll. Trusting can never give them cards.
variation.objective: After round 24, the player holding the fewest cards wins. If several players tie for fewest, the one with the most CATCHES wins. If still tied, the one with the fewest CAUGHT wins. If still tied, the game is a draw among those players.
variation.expected_effect: With only about 2.7 matching cards per hand, every player must bluff about 5 cards away in 8 turns. Each responder must weigh the claim size against the copies they can see (4 minus their own copies minus revealed copies) and against the growing pile. Calling a big pile is very costly if wrong, and so is letting a cheap bluff through. Simple policies lose. Always k=4 is almost always a bluff and swallows the pile. Always Challenge eats whole piles on true plays. Always Trust lets rivals shed freely while gaining nothing on the tiebreak. Always k=1 empties only if never caught, and cheap challenges punish it. Players disagree because only one can win: the active player's statement is a pure bluff tool, and each responder can hope the other challenges first. Ties at 0 are settled by challenge accuracy, so reading skill decides close games. The remaining seat effect (seat 1 moves first, onto an empty pile) should be checked in testing.

balanced.evidence:
Deck: 24 cards, ranks 1-4, six copies of each; 8 cards per hand. Hypergeometric odds for one hand: P(no copies of a given rank) = C(18,8)/C(24,8) = 43758/735471 = 0.059. P(at least 4 of a rank) = 0.0624 + 0.0067 + 0.0002 = 0.069. P(5 or more of a rank) is about 0.007 per rank, about 0.027 per hand.

Responder decision for one claim (cards gained by the responder; negative is good):
- k=1 claim (true about 94%): Trust = 0.94x0 + 0.06x(+1) = +0.06. Challenge = 0.94x(+1) + 0.06x(-1) = +0.88. Trust is better.
- k=4 claim (true about 7% unless the responder's own count rules it out): Trust = about 0.93x(+1) = +0.93. Challenge = 0.07x(+4) + 0.93x(-1) = about -0.65. Challenge is better.
So neither response is strictly better.

Thoughtless policies:
- Always k=4: about 93% bluffs, and any sensible responder challenges, so the bluffer swallows the pile. It loses.
- Always k=1: removes at most 1 card per turn and cannot empty before round 22. It loses.
- Always Challenge: takes k cards on every true play. It loses.
- 'Play k = my count of the required rank (true every time), always Trust': this is the real problem. The ranks rotate, so seat 1 faces 1,4,3,2 in rounds 1,4,7,10. Seat 2 faces 2,1,4,3 in rounds 2,5,8,11. Seat 3 faces 3,2,1,4 in rounds 3,6,9,12. A player with at most 4 of every rank (about 97%) can therefore dump the whole hand honestly within four turns, and nobody can profitably challenge.

Under this policy for all three players:
- Round-9 check: it fires only if a seat was dealt no copies of its fourth rank. That chance is about 1-(0.94)^3, roughly 17%, and it is a sole win only if exactly one seat lacks that rank.
- Round-12 check: otherwise all three hold 0 cards, or two hold 0 if someone was dealt 5+ of a rank. Under the WINNER RULE that is a draw.
Roughly 80% of games end as draws, and the honest-plus-trust policy essentially never loses against sensible opponents. Bluffing gains little because the honest route already empties you.

Seat edge: every end check (rounds 3,6,9,...) comes immediately after seat 3's turn. Seats 1 and 2, if they empty in rounds 10 and 11, must still answer seat 3's and each other's claims while at 0, where a wrong guess costs cards (Trust on a bluff gives +1, Challenge on a true play gives +k). Seat 3 never faces that exposure before a check. A second, smaller asymmetry: on a true play the first challenger in seat order takes exactly the k played cards, while the second takes the next k from deeper in the pile.

playable.evidence:
Completeness: the rules cover the empty hand (skip; removal of nothing), k larger than the hand, an empty or short pile when trusters draw, the challenger order, the pile as a stack, the deterministic order in which the engine picks cards (required rank, then the next ranks with wraparound), the tie rule and the end conditions. A model with only these words can act in every situation.

Finiteness: the game is finite (at most 24 rounds) and decided by arithmetic on hand counts.

Complexity: 13 steps (limit 20), 2 choice steps (limit 4), 11 attributes (limit 20), 2 hidden elements (hands, pile; limit 3), 0 random draws per round (the shuffle is at setup), 24 rounds (limit 40).

Cost: the card-selection rule and the 'fewest-held rank' removal need several calc/remove operations. They are flat, `when`-guarded and arithmetic, and plausibly fit within 20 steps.

Simultaneity and talk: the response is a simultaneous poll, as required. The active player's optional statement is a reasonable talk channel. Responders share an interest in catching bluffs and would gain little from pre-round talk, so its absence is defensible.

Restrictions: no board, clock, judge or trading is used.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
There is real inference available. A responder can cap the opponent's possible count using 6 minus their own copies minus revealed copies; a k=4 claim when you hold 3 of the rank is a certain bluff. Hand-size tracking also helps.

Under the intended good strategy (play your true count, trust plausible claims, challenge impossible ones), no one needs to bluff, because each seat meets every rank within its first four turns. The result is then:
- about 80% draws at round 12, or
- a win at round 9 decided purely by which player happened to be dealt no copies of their fourth-faced rank.
The winner is therefore set by the deal or not at all, and a good reasoner is not clearly favoured over a merely honest one. I estimate chance and draws decide well over half of the results.

required_changes: Force bluffing so that inference matters. Use ranks 1-6 with 4 copies each (still 24 cards) and keep the required rank at ((r-1) mod 6)+1, with the engine's wraparound counting 6 as followed by 1. Each seat then always faces the same two ranks (seat 1: 1 and 4, seat 2: 2 and 5, seat 3: 3 and 6), so roughly two-thirds of every hand can only leave through bluffs, which opponents must read using card counting.

Remove the seat-3 edge from check timing. Replace the 'multiple of 3' early end with a single fixed end after round 24. Alternatively, run the end check after every round and end the game when any player reaches 0, with the winner being the player who emptied first.
Cut the draw rate. Add an arithmetic tiebreak for tied fewest cards: first, more successful challenges (bluffs caught); then, fewer times caught bluffing; draw only if still tied.
Remove the first/second challenger asymmetry on true plays: each challenger takes ceil(k/2) cards from the top, or both take k, so seat order does not matter.

balanced.evidence:
STRUCTURE. The active player's only choice is k. The engine picks the cards, so a play is TRUE exactly when the player holds at least k cards of the required rank. Challengers choose Trust or Challenge.

CHALLENGER PAYOFFS (change in your own hand; pile size P includes the k cards just played):
| You \ other challenger | Trust | Challenge |
|---|---|---|
| Trust, play TRUE | 0 | 0 |
| Trust, play BLUFF | 0 (the bluffer sheds k) | 0 (the bluffer takes P) |
| Challenge, play TRUE | +P | +floor(P/2) |
| Challenge, play BLUFF | 0 and CATCHES+1 (the bluffer takes P) | same |

No option is dominant. Trust never adds cards to you, but letting a bluff through lets a rival shed k cards, which loses you ground under 'fewest cards wins'. Challenge gives the bluffer +P when right and costs you +P when wrong. The decision therefore depends on your estimate of P(bluff).

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the winner rule:
(1) Always k=4. A play is TRUE only if you hold all 4 copies of the rank (very rare at deal). Any opponent holding one copy knows it is a bluff and challenges, so you take P each time. You lose to sensible play. Against random challengers (each challenges with probability 1/2, so at least one challenges 3/4 of the time) you are caught about 75% of the time and usually lose.
(2) Always k=1. This sheds at most 1 card per activation, so 8 cards reach 0 only at your final activation (rounds 22, 23 or 24), and only if you are never caught. Any catch adds P. Even at 0 cards you have 0 CATCHES, so any opponent who also reaches 0 with one catch beats you on the tiebreak. It can lose.
(3) Always Trust. You never gain cards as challenger, but rivals bluff through freely when the other rival also trusts, and you earn no CATCHES. You lose ties and races to rivals who shed faster.
(4) Always Challenge. Every TRUE play (an honest player plays exactly their count) gives you P or P/2. You lose heavily to honest play.
(5) Random. Loses to calibrated challenging.
No thoughtless policy avoids losing.

ALL-TRUST DEGENERACY. If everyone always trusts, everyone plays k=4 and all reach 0 by round 6, giving a 3-way draw. That is not stable: anyone holding a copy of the claimed rank challenges a k=4 claim with certainty and dumps P on the bluffer.

SEATS. The rank assignment is symmetric: each seat owns 2 ranks (8 of 24 cards) and has 8 activations.
- Seat 1 opens round 1 onto an empty pile, so a caught round-1 bluff costs only the k cards back plus CAUGHT+1. This is a small edge, offset by giving opponents CATCHES.
- Seat 3 acts last (round 24) and must play at least 1 card if it holds any. Seats 1 and 2 face the same forced final exposure in rounds 22 and 23.
- Any player who empties a pile hands the next active player the same cheap-bluff spot, so the edge rotates rather than being seat-locked.

All three seats can realistically win. Hypergeometric own-rank count at deal (N=24, K=8, n=8): mean 2.67, standard deviation about 1.1, P(0) about 1.7%.

This is not a cooperation game, so the 'higher total' cooperation trap does not apply. In round 24 Trust is not a free win: trusting a bluff lets the active seat shed and possibly win.

playable.evidence:
RULES ARE COMPLETE.
- The seat and rank formulas are checked: r=1 gives seat 1 rank 1, r=4 gives seat 1 rank 4, r=24 gives seat 3 rank 6.
- Card selection is deterministic: required rank first, then the next rank up, wrapping 6 to 1.
- k is capped at hand size, and a 0-card player skips.
- All three challenge outcomes are specified, including the odd card removed when two challengers split.
- 0-card players still answer polls.
- Game length is fixed at 24 rounds, and the winner is decided by arithmetic on numbers the game keeps: hand size, then CATCHES, then CAUGHT, then draw.

NO FORBIDDEN FEATURES. No board, clock, judge, trading or binding agreement. The challenge decision is a simultaneous poll, as required.

LIMITS:
| Item | Design | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| steps_per_round | 11 | 20 |
| choice_steps_per_round | 2 (k, poll) | 4 |
| attributes | 16 (3 hands, 6 counters, pile, removed pile, round, active seat, rank, k, truth flag) | 20 |
| hidden_elements | 2 (hands, pile) | 3 |
| random_draws_per_round | 1 (only the 6(c) shuffle) | 1 |
| rounds | 24 | 40 |

TALK (3 players). The only talk is the active player's single public statement before the simultaneous poll. This is placed where interests conflict: the active player wants Trust and the challengers want to catch bluffs. Believing a false statement costs the listener P cards, so it gives challengers something to reason about. It is not a follow-the-leader proposal. Challengers do not need a talk step: their poll outcome depends mainly on the active player's honesty, not on coordinating with each other.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE ENTERS THREE WAYS.
- The initial deal: own-rank count has mean 2.67 and standard deviation about 1.1.
- Which cards arrive in pile pickups.
- The 6(c) shuffle.

SKILL ENTERS SEVERAL WAYS.
(a) Choosing k. Truth requires holding at least k, and honest k leaks your count, so choosing between k = count and a bluff of count+1 is a real decision.
(b) Card counting. There are 4 copies of each rank. Revealed challenge cards, your own holdings and the fixed rank-to-seat mapping bound what the active player can hold. Example: if you hold 3 ones, seat 1's claim of 2 ones is certainly a bluff.
(c) Pile-size timing. Bluff when the pile is small, for example right after a pickup. Challenge when the pile is large and your evidence of a bluff is strong.
(d) Opponent modelling. Weigh the free-text statement and the other challenger's likely poll.

GOOD PLAY BY EVERYONE. Each player plays honest or small-bluff k and challenges only on high bluff probability. The result is then decided by who gets caught and who catches, including the CATCHES tiebreak when several players reach 0. That outcome turns on inference quality, not on a single hidden draw. A bad deal (few own-rank cards) can be overcome through low-k bluffs timed onto small piles and accurate challenges.

ESTIMATE. Roughly 30-40% of the outcome is chance. A reasoning player is clearly favoured over a random or thoughtless one, as shown by policies (1) to (5) under balanced.

triage.reason: The game was built correctly, but the design fails evaluation on two counts. A round has 6 choice steps against a limit of 4, and a thoughtless 'always take the first option' policy wins about 77–80% of its games from either seat while 'always take the last option' loses about 75–80%, so a trivial strategy dominates.
triage.guidance: Cut the choice steps per round to at most 4. Drop the separate free-text talk step, or fold talk into the play step, so each turn is one play choice plus one simultaneous challenge poll. If the 4-player count still exceeds the limit, count a round as one turn rather than a full cycle. Then rebalance so no fixed option ordering wins. As written, playing 1 card while never challenging, or a similar first-option default, is safe and strong: playing few cards rarely costs much, and challenging risks taking the whole pile. Options to try: (1) Require a minimum play that grows with pile size, or set the minimum at 2 when the player holds enough cards, so slow-dumping 1 card is not free. (2) Lessen the challenger's risk on a true claim, for example the challenger takes only the cards just played rather than the whole pile, so challenging bluffs is worthwhile and constant bluffing or constant passing is punished. (3) Make the challenge decision count for the player who challenges against a bluff, for example the challenger subtracts the revealed cards from their taken counter. Re-check that neither all-first nor all-last policies win clearly above the random baseline of about one third.

triage.reason: In the final state seat 2 has hand_size 1, catches 2 and caught 1. The required formula gives 0 - 10000 + 200 - 1 = -9801, which is exactly what the game reported, so the game is right and the test's expected -9901 is an arithmetic error.
triage.guidance: Recompute R19's expected standings from the rank_by formula `0 - hand_size*10000 + catches*100 - caught`, using the counters seat 2 actually ends with. All players chose Trust in the final round, so no counter can change; with catches 2 and caught 1 the value is -9801, not -9901. To show that fewer caught breaks the tie, set the given state so both tied seats have equal hand_size and equal catches. Then check that the seat with fewer caught has the higher standing and wins, rather than hard-coding a miscalculated number.
